headline: Genetic analysis links air pollutants to lung disease and higher Alzheimer's risk
dek: A new study suggests polluted air may affect the brain through the lungs, according to a summary by WHO technical officer Dr Alexey Kulikov.
body:
A new study suggests that polluted air may reach the brain through the lungs, Dr Alexey Kulikov, a Technical Officer in the WHO Department of NCDs and Mental Health, wrote in a post on X.

According to his summary, the researchers found that genetic liability to exposure to PM2.5, PM10, NO2 and NOx was causally associated with asthma, COPD, emphysema, pulmonary fibrosis and lung cancer. It was also associated with reduced lung function and a higher risk of Alzheimer's disease.

Kulikov said the authors propose a mechanism in which emphysema and COPD lower levels of soluble LRP1, a receptor that clears amyloid-beta from the brain. The inflammation markers IL-6 and MMP-9 drive this process, he wrote. Lower LRP1 in turn raises IL-6 and MMP-9 again, which feeds back into lung damage.

Kulikov noted that the results are genetic inferences drawn from summary-level data. He said experimental and clinical work is still needed before the proposed pathways can guide treatment.

In his view, the findings add to the case that clean air and good COPD care could also help protect against dementia.
key_quote: emphysema and COPD lower soluble LRP1, a receptor that clears amyloid-beta from the brain
